title: The same opening range rules made 1,582% on NQ and zeroed the account on ES
author: person-person12
selftext:
Opening range breakout is about the most taught intraday setup there is, and almost every result you ever see quoted for it is quoted on the Nasdaq. So I took one set of rules and ran them across three different markets over the same dates, changing nothing else.

The rules: mark the first fifteen minutes after the open, buy the break of the range high, stop under the range, target a multiple of it, flat at the close, longs only. 5 minute candles, may 2016 through march 2026, 100k to start, with commission and slippage charged against every entry and every exit. I ran all three in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading) so the same code and the same cost assumptions carried across.

**NQ:** 1,802 trades, 48.8% wins, profit factor 1.15, **+1,582%**, worst drawdown **80.67%**

**ES:** 740 trades, 43.7% wins, profit factor 0.94, **account at zero on march 24 2020**

**Gold:** 117 trades, 36.8% wins, profit factor 0.54, **account at zero in january 2017**

Same rules in all three. On the Nasdaq it turns 100k into 1.68m, and on the S&P it is dead before the covid selloff has even finished.

**\_\_\_\_\_**

The ES year split is the part I keep looking at. 2017, 2018 and 2019 it ground out a small profit every year at a profit factor sitting around 1.05, which is exactly the kind of result that keeps somebody trading a thing. Then 52 trades into 2020 it lost 122k and there was nothing left in the account.

The Nasdaq run isnt the win it looks like either. **It drew down 80.67%** on the way to that 1,582%. An account falling from 400k to 77k before it recovers is fine as a line on a chart and no person alive sits through it, and every prop eval going would have closed it years before the good years showed up.

**\_\_\_\_\_**

What causes the split is that the rules never say anything about which market theyre for. The opening range on NQ is wide, so a stop under it clears the normal noise after the open. That same shaped stop on gold sits right on top of price, so you get knocked out of trades that would otherwise have paid, and the winners left over dont cover the losers. Nothing in the rulebook knows any of that, and a backtest on NQ on its own is never going to mention it.

Its a recipe written at sea level. Same steps and same ingredients, and it comes out wrong in Denver, and the recipe doesnt contain the part that explains why.

The cheapest check on anything youre running is the same rules on a market they were not written for. These ones lasted eight months on gold.
